Unfortunately, winter maintenance is severely lacking. Last winter, I walked from Rosedale
Mall on the north side of County Road B2 to Fairview and along Fairview to Blick Art
Supplies. NONE of the north sidewalk on B2 was shoveled so I had to trudge through the
snow. The various businesses had paid to have their parking lots plowed but no one had
bothered to plow the sidewalk. So I walked through the bank parking lot hoping that Fairview
east sidewalk would be plowed but it was even worse. So I was forced to cross Fairview in
the middle of the street (5 lanes of traffic) to get to a sidewalk on the other side. I am an able
bodied person and none of these streets were accessible to me. In a wheelchair, I'd have to
leave the county in the winter or I couldn't survive. When sidewalks are plowed, street plows
often pile up berms of snow in the crosswalks near ADA ramps or curbs, making crossing the
street impossible. Gotta plow street first and sidewalk second and include the crosswalks

This has the tendency of becoming car-centric rather than pedestrian and ADA centric. That’s
because streets are often prioritized in County plans and TIPs based on road surface condition
rather than where pedestrian and ADA improvements are most needed. For example, Snelling
Avenue between Hewitt and Como is a critical bike/ped link but it’s not ADA accessible and is
also unsafe for pedestrians and cyclists. Most sidewalks are just 5 feet wide with power poles or
other obstacles in the middle of them–not enough space for a pedestrian or cyclist to safely
pass a wheelchair (or other cyclist) going in the opposite direction. Traffic speeds average
50mph and crosswalks at on/off-ramps have poor visibility/sightlines. MnDOT has 60% plan
sets to fix this stretch (I’ve seen them) but Ramsey County and Saint Paul need to make it a
priority so ADA and bike/ped improvements can happen. Yet it’s not high on their priority lists
because pavement and bridge condition is considered “good”.

The mindset here is completely backwards. The statement intrinsically prioritizes automobiles
and then tacks on pedestrian facilities at the end. In practice, this is how the county operates
during the design phase of the project. “You don’t really need bike lanes on BOTH sides of the
road.” Yes, we do. Please stop envisioning these projects as road projects. They are
transportation projects. To prioritize walking and biking (as the county pretends to do), the
mindset should be: “How many cars can we allow into this space without infringing on the ability
of pedestrians and cyclists to get around.” Center non-car travel!

Public Works staff? Why not the public? There has to be some way to rank all the county roads
by how busy they are with autos, bikers & pedestrians.

Coordination – I think Ramsey County needs to work with all the other agencies listed to
eliminate barriers along its own routes. This is a major issue for some country roads that are the
backbone of the arterial and collector system in cities such as Saint Paul. It shouldn’t be the

city’s job to push the county to make things accessible on its own system. You reference the
county TIP. I think Ramsey County needs to take a long hard look at its cost participation policy,
which pushes costs to local agencies for sidewalk and shared use path construction. Again, this
is for NEW facilities within Ramsey County right of way. This doesn’t make sense. You can’t
say you’re building for accessibility and then throw up financial barriers to implementing
accessibility. And those are real barriers for local agencies to pony up 50% of costs for new
facilities on county roads. Regarding current ADA standards: I would urge the county to go
beyond this when necessary. E.g. 4’ walks are too narrow.

The grievance procedure is laughable. RC gets to decide what is worthy of their time and
effort when it is the people using the facilities that know precisely what’s wrong with the
facilities. There should be people who use wheelchairs, power scooters, walkers, crutches,
canes or have prosthetic devices on every one of these committees that have an equal say in
how things are designed. The current plans for the sidewalk aprons are inadequate as RC
has been repeatedly told by persons using narrow-wheeled devices, crutches, canes or
prosthetic devices as it is VERY easy for these items to get caught in the textured surfaces
and cause falls. One simple question to individuals using these devices would have saved a
huge amount of money in the design phase. Poorly done and now no one is willing to hear
what these individuals are trying to say. The grievance process is already (still) broken.
